SHUTDOWN SA

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa has been ravaged by mayhem and destruction in a week of violent looting - what started off as proZuma campaign shifted to anarchy and economic sabotage. We track the devastation and loss

Summary:
As the country went up in flames. We hit the streets to capture the devastation, the trauma and question the motives behind what has been described as economic sabotage.





Further information:
We cover the riots in Durban and JHB – capturing the biggest riots in the country since the dawn of democracy. We humanise the devastation by speaking to people impacted, we go into the hardest hit areas with security teams who are reeling from the onslaught protesters turned looters.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: This week saw South Africa go up in flames. Indiscriminate looting left shopping centres wrecked, warehouses destroyed, distribution centres ransacked and infrastructure torched.

LINK: IT started as a freeZuma campaign but soon spiralled out of control as masses took to the streets and destroyed everything in their path with complete disregard for the law.

VO: For ten days now, South Africa has been reeling from the chaos – the mayhem – and utter destruction.

By Monday morning, trucks were burnt; freeways blocked, small businesses and entire shopping malls taken out in KZN.

DEVEN: They are unstoppable, not a bullet, not a rubber bullet, not a live ammunition will stop them. They want to loot. They want to steal.

VO: Deven Pillay has been responding to scenes across Durban.

DEVEN: They feel that they are making their lives better and they are not making their lives better because they are stealing from the same people that support them every single day.

VO: Raven Kisten’s butchery was looted by some of his very own customers. We met him just as he arrived to see the aftermath.

RAVEN: Right now I’m more in shocked….yesterday when we left the shop, not thinking that today you wouldn't have one. But it's just heartbreaking. It's heartbreaking to see and know they're doing their community. Couldn't stand beside you here.

VO: While former president Jacob Zuma’s incarceration was most likely the catalyst, there is still no real clarity on what the driving forces behind the unprecedented looting are.

ZIYANDA: I think I think we would really be amiss to try and dismiss this as as either just a proZUMA camp or just opportunistic criminals or or people who are desperate. what we have at the moment, unfortunately, is sort of very wicked brew of all of those groups coming together at once.

VO: Researcher and Policy Analyst Ziyanda Stuurman believes it’s a scenario that’s been brewing for years.

ZIYANDA: What we're seeing is is, again, the sort of perfect storm of a lost decade of economic growth in the Zuma years and erosion of government and government services again during the state capture years and and growing sort of inequality and unemployment. And that didn't happen overnight.

VO: To see the devastation first hand, our crew was escorted into Central Durban by Fidelity’s specialist intervention unit.

JOHAN: Always need to be alert. Never know what's around the corner

VO: Johan Pretorius had been on the frontlines all night.

JOHAN: there's not enough resources to combat this crime. We need a lot more support as we can. we're not enough. We're not enough.

VO: The streets were chaotic with people shamelessly scurrying off with their loot.

Pretorius took us inside a shopping centre in the suburb of Glenwood. The looters were still at it.

JOHAN: Hey! Get down! GETDOWN

VO: Retail outlets were annihilated by looters predominantly in Durban and Pietermartizburg.

JOHAN: They start to get violent as well – they tell you straight what are you going to do
UPSOUND POLICEMAN: PHUMA! PHUMA!

VO: Fidelity Services Group covers 85% of malls across South AFrica, CEO Wahl Bartmann says the private security sector is under pressure.

WAHL: this is in a totally different level. I think we've dealt a lot with riots, we've dealt with some looting. But but this is just to the next level.

LINK: AS THE WEEK WENT ON WITH A RELATIVELY LOW NUMBER OF ARRESTS, LOOTERS GREW BRAVER AND MORE BRAZEN – NOT AT ALL PHASED BY CAMERAS, OR ARMED LAW ENFORCEMENT – THEY SET THEIR SIGHTS ON BIGGER TARGETS AND BECAME MORE ORGANISED

MARTIN: I've never seen such looting, such devastation, such trashing of businesses.

VO: We took to the sky with Martin Coetzer, a pilot who’s worked in private security for more than two decades.

UPSOUND MARTIN: have you ever seen anything like this in your life? Look at this?

VO: Looters came in vehicles causing traffic jams as they stole more than they could carry – [scenes emerging from Durban felt almost apocalyptic]

The riots spread to Gauteng, with mobs targeting small local businesses, major retail outlets and malls in mostly low income areas in and around Johannesburg and Pretoria.

We ventured into Alexandra Township, bordering Sandton, with a Private Security Team that’s been working alongside the police and military. Shane Theunissen says it’s been tough, as the violence has escalated.

SHANE: They come at us from all angles.
MAC: do you feel that the looters know you’re hands are tied.
SHANE: They know that the right to life supersedes that of theft, you know, they know that we can't shoot them for theft. So it makes our lives very difficult.

VO: The looters are coming armed, taking security teams head on - the main goal is to keep the looters from getting in, explains Bartmann.

WAHL: Masses of people coming towards you, you need to be able to deal with them and once they've entered into the site and they've gained entry to it, it's so difficult to stop it. So when before they get into that site, that's where we need to respond.

LINK: SCENES OF INDISCRIMINATE LOOTING AND LAWLESSNESS HIGHLIGHTED THE POLICE’S INABILITY TO DEAL WITH THIS LEVEL OF ANARCHY – THEY WERE OVER WHELMED, OVER POWERED AND OVER RUN IN MANY SITUATIONS.

XOLANI: This country is not being governed // it has been on autopilot for the past twenty seven years.

VO: Political Commentator Xolani Dube believes government has failed the country.

XOLANI: That's the fact is the private security guards, // communities are protecting themselves. People are protecting their own properties, where is the state?

VO: Communities all over Durban barricaded entrances to their suburbs, and in some cases they’ve even gone to protect their local retailers from looters.

ROY: We've got everyone and they've they've come to bring trucks to block off roads. They've people we've never met.

VO: Store owners like Roy Keyter have been overwhelmed by the support from community members who came out to stand guard after looters tried to hit his outlet earlier.

ROY: it wasn't about the store, it wasn't about losing the stock. It was just more about what was happening in the community. it's it's it's not me, its us. So I think that's touched a nerve

UPSOUND: WE WILL DEFEND IT WITH EVERYTHING THAT WE HAVE

VO: Communities all over the country have come out to protect retail infrastructure from Durban to Tembisa.

But as Tension mounts in some areas, violence and attacks on looters have been reported, with at least 15 people killed this week in Phoenix, Durban.

Communities have been warned about taking the law into their own hands. This is a clip from Deputy Minister of State Security, Zizi Kodwa.

ZIZI: But it is beginning to have an element of vigilantism, it could lead to racial tension which again is what instigators also planned.

VO: Government Agencies have identified a list of so-called instigators. Kodwa believes there are more sinister driving forces at work here.

ZIZI: what we see now, // a clear orchestrated plan of economical sabotage for very ulterior motives to destablise the country so that at the end there must be popular revolt to remove this government lead by President Ramaphosa because of the stance President Ramaphosa has taken on corruption.

VO: According to Kodwa, initial threats focussed on critical infrastructure, which prompted the deployment of 2500 SANDF members in Gauteng and KZN. The number is now set to increase to 25 000 following the extent of the riots.

While many citizens breathed a sigh of relief - Stuurman doesn’t believe normalising military reaction to social unrest and criminal incidents, is a good thing.

ZIYANDA: I think that that we're headed down a very, very dangerous path of calling in the military more and more often // what it means and what it says about the capability and capacity of the police to deal with with incidents and with situations that are part of their job.

VO: By the end of the week, around 200 people had died, more than 2200 had been arrested including some of the alleged instigators, while others were still under surveillance. Police Minister Bheki Cele insists the police are on top of matters.

CELE: The police msut spend time to quell the situation - we are not going to leave them

VO: As the looting continued for most of the week, the gravity of the destruction started to set in with billions of rands in losses.

Around 100 malls damaged, at least 800 stores looted - this includes at least 90 pharmacies and more than 200 liquor stores and. Restaurants targeted. ATMs raided, warehouses and distribution centres destroyed, pharmaceutical manufacturers set alight, schools wrecked.

Unable to get their goods to end users, farmers have been forced to dump produce. SAPREF has halted fuel production. Afrox has halted gas deliveries. A number of terminals have been shut at Durban Port. Global logistics company, Maersk shutdown all of its depots, warehouses and coldstores. SASSA Payments have been put on hold. Some Banks and ATMs have stopped operations. Big corporates have closed their offices as a precautionary measure around the country.

Parts of the N3 were closed off for most of the week, [preventing the transit of people and supplies].

GAVIN: It's been absolute carnage out on the roads, there's just no other word for this.

VO: The transport industry estimates between 200 to 300 million rand in lost assets and cargo alone, according Gavin Kelly from the Road Freight Association.

GAVIN: If we don’t stop that, and It has to be stopped now, if we don't stop that, it would mean. The whole logistics network will collapse. The distribution centers are being looted. So there's no stock at the back gate to bring to them to the local shop near you. We are going to see food shortages coming into play. That's the harsh reality.

VO: Already, fuel is in short supply, cars lined up for kilometers as most petrol stations were closed in Durban this week. Government announced that buying petrol and diesel in a container is now illegal.

Food supplies are also limited particularly in KZN, where people are queuing for hours at the few grocery stores that were spared by looters.

In the days to come, food, fuel and other critical aid destined for KwaZulu-Natal will be transported in armed police convoys.

LINK: THE TRUE EXTENT OF THE DESTRUCTION HAS NOT BEEN SEEN YET, THE ECONOMY WILL NOT BOUNCE BACK FROM THIS QUICKLY. THE CONSEQUENCES WILL BE FAR REACHING AND THE REMANENCE OF THE LOOTING WILL BE FELT LONG AFTER THE FIRES HAVE DIED OUT.

GAVIN: Somebody has to pay to cover the damages to get everything back, And what sort of costs are they going to be so fat? And who pays for that? You and I.

XOLANI: We have never been in hell all of us whites, blacks and indians, never been in this sinkhole is for the first time everyone is vulnerable, this is is for the first time post democracy in a modern society.

VO: Dube firmly blames government, or rather the lack of it, for the scenes that gripped the nation this week.

XOLANI: we don't to have a government. We just had crooks who have been, pillaging us for years . the people are stealing from us, can't provide us with solutions because they thrive on chaos. If the society is stable, they become the victim because we always ask for accountability

VO: And international investor confidence in South Africa would have taken a serious blow as images of anarchy flew around the globe.

GAVIN: It's no longer a safe, reliable, efficient. Country where you can move goods through. I think we are going to lose billions of rands in terms of lost trade opportunities.

VO: Dube believes if we are to survive this, we will have to dig deep and unite.

XOLANI: we can rise and become a powerful nation. But if we are not going to do that. I can assure you we're not going to raise this country's going to be Mogadishu. now if we're not going to do it sooner we are going to have electricity, sooner. We're not going to be able to communicate, sooner we are not going to have water - we need to prevent that situation now.

MAC: CAN WE COMe back from this?
ZIYANDA: We have no choice. Do we do we kind of throw our hands in the air and say, well, that's the end of the country, you know? Thanks for trying. I mean, we have to we have to we have to find our way back from this.

VO: While clean up operations around the country have started, communities are coming out in their numbers to reclaim their streets, authorities have started going from door to door in some of the affected areas to retrieve looted items.

ROY: When we hit the bottom as a time to run towards that, not to run away, this is the time for us all to get together, embrace and remember how beautiful our land is and standing together. And let's fix this. And it's all of us get to the finish line and get this country back to where it should be.

Never know what's around the corner VO: Johan Pretorius had been on the frontlines all night. JOHAN: there's not enough resources to combat this crime. We need a lot more support as we can. we're not enough. We're not enough. VO: The streets were chaotic with people shamelessly scurrying off with their loot. Pretorius took us inside a shopping centre in the suburb of Glenwood. The looters were still at it. JOHAN: Hey! Get down! GETDOWN VO: Retail outlets were annihilated by looters predominantly in Durban and Pietermartizburg. JOHAN: They start to get violent as well – they tell you straight what are you going to do UPSOUND POLICEMAN: PHUMA! PHUMA! VO: Fidelity Services Group covers 85% of malls across South AFrica, CEO Wahl Bartmann says the private security sector is under pressure. WAHL: this is in a totally different level. I think we've dealt a lot with riots, we've dealt with some looting. But but this is just to the next level. LINK: AS THE WEEK WENT ON WITH A RELATIVELY LOW NUMBER OF ARRESTS, LOOTERS GREW BRAVER AND MORE BRAZEN – NOT AT ALL PHASED BY CAMERAS, OR ARMED LAW ENFORCEMENT – THEY SET THEIR SIGHTS ON BIGGER TARGETS AND BECAME MORE ORGANISED MARTIN: I've never seen such looting, such devastation, such trashing of businesses. VO: We took to the sky with Martin Coetzer, a pilot who’s worked in private security for more than two decades. UPSOUND MARTIN: have you ever seen anything like this in your life? Look at this? VO: Looters came in vehicles causing traffic jams as they stole more than they could carry – [scenes emerging from Durban felt almost apocalyptic] The riots spread to Gauteng, with mobs targeting small local businesses, major retail outlets and malls in mostly low income areas in and around Johannesburg and Pretoria. We ventured into Alexandra Township, bordering Sandton, with a Private Security Team that’s been working alongside the police and military. Shane Theunissen says it’s been tough, as the violence has escalated. SHANE: They come at us from all angles. MAC: do you feel that the looters know you’re hands are tied. SHANE: They know that the right to life supersedes that of theft, you know, they know that we can't shoot them for theft. So it makes our lives very difficult. VO: The looters are coming armed, taking security teams head on - the main goal is to keep the looters from getting in, explains Bartmann. WAHL: Masses of people coming towards you, you need to be able to deal with them and once they've entered into the site and they've gained entry to it, it's so difficult to stop it. So when before they get into that site, that's where we need to respond. LINK: SCENES OF INDISCRIMINATE LOOTING AND LAWLESSNESS HIGHLIGHTED THE POLICE’S INABILITY TO DEAL WITH THIS LEVEL OF ANARCHY – THEY WERE OVER WHELMED, OVER POWERED AND OVER RUN IN MANY SITUATIONS. XOLANI: This country is not being governed // it has been on autopilot for the past twenty seven years. VO: Political Commentator Xolani Dube believes government has failed the country. XOLANI: That's the fact is the private security guards, // communities are protecting themselves. People are protecting their own properties, where is the state? VO: Communities all over Durban barricaded entrances to their suburbs, and in some cases they’ve even gone to protect their local retailers from looters. ROY: We've got everyone and they've they've come to bring trucks to block off roads. They've people we've never met. VO: Store owners like Roy Keyter have been overwhelmed by the support from community members who came out to stand guard after looters tried to hit his outlet earlier. ROY: it wasn't about the store, it wasn't about losing the stock. It was just more about what was happening in the community. it's it's it's not me, its us. So I think that's touched a nerve UPSOUND: WE WILL DEFEND IT WITH EVERYTHING THAT WE HAVE VO: Communities all over the country have come out to protect retail infrastructure from Durban to Tembisa. But as Tension mounts in some areas, violence and attacks on looters have been reported, with at least 15 people killed this week in Phoenix, Durban. Communities have been warned about taking the law into their own hands. This is a clip from Deputy Minister of State Security, Zizi Kodwa. ZIZI: But it is beginning to have an element of vigilantism, it could lead to racial tension which again is what instigators also planned. VO: Government Agencies have identified a list of so-called instigators. Kodwa believes there are more sinister driving forces at work here. ZIZI: what we see now, // a clear orchestrated plan of economical sabotage for very ulterior motives to destablise the country so that at the end there must be popular revolt to remove this government lead by President Ramaphosa because of the stance President Ramaphosa has taken on corruption. VO: According to Kodwa, initial threats focussed on critical infrastructure, which prompted the deployment of 2500 SANDF members in Gauteng and KZN. The number is now set to increase to 25 000 following the extent of the riots. While many citizens breathed a sigh of relief - Stuurman doesn’t believe normalising military reaction to social unrest and criminal incidents, is a good thing. ZIYANDA: I think that that we're headed down a very, very dangerous path of calling in the military more and more often // what it means and what it says about the capability and capacity of the police to deal with with incidents and with situations that are part of their job. VO: By the end of the week, around 200 people had died, more than 2200 had been arrested including some of the alleged instigators, while others were still under surveillance. Police Minister Bheki Cele insists the police are on top of matters. CELE: The police msut spend time to quell the situation - we are not going to leave them VO: As the looting continued for most of the week, the gravity of the destruction started to set in with billions of rands in losses. Around 100 malls damaged, at least 800 stores looted - this includes at least 90 pharmacies and more than 200 liquor stores and. Restaurants targeted. ATMs raided, warehouses and distribution centres destroyed, pharmaceutical manufacturers set alight, schools wrecked. Unable to get their goods to end users, farmers have been forced to dump produce. SAPREF has halted fuel production. Afrox has halted gas deliveries. A number of terminals have been shut at Durban Port. Global logistics company, Maersk shutdown all of its depots, warehouses and coldstores. SASSA Payments have been put on hold. Some Banks and ATMs have stopped operations. Big corporates have closed their offices as a precautionary measure around the country. Parts of the N3 were closed off for most of the week, [preventing the transit of people and supplies]. GAVIN: It's been absolute carnage out on the roads, there's just no other word for this. VO: The transport industry estimates between 200 to 300 million rand in lost assets and cargo alone, according Gavin Kelly from the Road Freight Association. GAVIN: If we don’t stop that, and It has to be stopped now, if we don't stop that, it would mean. The whole logistics network will collapse. The distribution centers are being looted. So there's no stock at the back gate to bring to them to the local shop near you. We are going to see food shortages coming into play. That's the harsh reality. VO: Already, fuel is in short supply, cars lined up for kilometers as most petrol stations were closed in Durban this week. Government announced that buying petrol and diesel in a container is now illegal. Food supplies are also limited particularly in KZN, where people are queuing for hours at the few grocery stores that were spared by looters. In the days to come, food, fuel and other critical aid destined for KwaZulu-Natal will be transported in armed police convoys. LINK: THE TRUE EXTENT OF THE DESTRUCTION HAS NOT BEEN SEEN YET, THE ECONOMY WILL NOT BOUNCE BACK FROM THIS QUICKLY. THE CONSEQUENCES WILL BE FAR REACHING AND THE REMANENCE OF THE LOOTING WILL BE FELT LONG AFTER THE FIRES HAVE DIED OUT. GAVIN: Somebody has to pay to cover the damages to get everything back, And what sort of costs are they going to be so fat? And who pays for that? You and I. XOLANI: We have never been in hell all of us whites, blacks and indians, never been in this sinkhole is for the first time everyone is vulnerable, this is is for the first time post democracy in a modern society. VO: Dube firmly blames government, or rather the lack of it, for the scenes that gripped the nation this week. XOLANI: we don't to have a government. We just had crooks who have been, pillaging us for years . the people are stealing from us, can't provide us with solutions because they thrive on chaos. If the society is stable, they become the victim because we always ask for accountability VO: And international investor confidence in South Africa would have taken a serious blow as images of anarchy flew around the globe. GAVIN: It's no longer a safe, reliable, efficient. Country where you can move goods through. I think we are going to lose billions of rands in terms of lost trade opportunities. VO: Dube believes if we are to survive this, we will have to dig deep and unite. XOLANI: we can rise and become a powerful nation. But if we are not going to do that. I can assure you we're not going to raise this country's going to be Mogadishu. now if we're not going to do it sooner we are going to have electricity, sooner. We're not going to be able to communicate, sooner we are not going to have water - we need to prevent that situation now. MAC: CAN WE COMe back from this? ZIYANDA: We have no choice. Do we do we kind of throw our hands in the air and say, well, that's the end of the country, you know? Thanks for trying. I mean, we have to we have to we have to find our way back from this. VO: While clean up operations around the country have started, communities are coming out in their numbers to reclaim their streets, authorities have started going from door to door in some of the affected areas to retrieve looted items. ROY: When we hit the bottom as a time to run towards that, not to run away, this is the time for us all to get together, embrace and remember how beautiful our land is and standing together. And let's fix this. And it's all of us get to the finish line and get this country back to where it should be. PROMO 1 – 21 seconds VO: FROM DURBAN TO JOHANNESBURG, THE COUNTRY was BURNING – SHOPPING MALLS HAVE BEEN LOOTED, WAREHOUSES RANSACKED AND THE ECONOMY CRIPPLED - Is it hunger, political support or just lawlessness? UPSOUND LOOTING ZIYANDA: What we're seeing is, the sort of perfect storm of a lost decade of economic growth in the Zuma years PROMO 2 – 21 seconds VO: Images of indiscriminate looting and violent riots gripped the country this week. MARTIN: I've never seen such looting, such devastation, such trashing of businesses. UPSOUND MARTIN: have you ever seen anything like this in your life? Look at this? VO: We hit the streets to capture the devastation, the trauma and question the motives behind what has been described as economic sabotage. PROMO 3 VO: South Africa has been ravaged by mayhem and destruction in a week of violent looting - what started off as proZuma campaign shifted to anarchy and economic sabotage. We track the devastation and losses.

metadata.Summary: As the country went up in flames. We hit the streets to capture the devastation, the trauma and question the motives behind what has been described as economic sabotage.
metadata.Further information: We cover the riots in Durban and JHB – capturing the biggest riots in the country since the dawn of democracy. We humanise the devastation by speaking to people impacted, we go into the hardest hit areas with security teams who are reeling from the onslaught protesters turned looters.
